etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed into Middle English in the 14th century from Old French variable, from Latin variare (“to change”), from varius (“different, various”). Equates to English vary +‎ -able.

definitions.definition: Able to vary or be varied.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.

definitions.definition: (biology) Tending to deviate from a normal or recognized type.
Something whose value may be dictated or discovered.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, Katie L. Burke, “In the News”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 193:
quote.text: Bats host many high-profile viruses that can infect humans, including severe acute respiratory syndrome and Ebola. A recent study explored the ecological variables that may contribute to bats’ propensity to harbor such zoonotic diseases by comparing them with another order of common reservoir hosts: rodents.

definitions.definition: English Wikipedia has an article on:Variable (mathematics)Wikipedia  (mathematics) A quantity that may assume any one of a set of values.
(programming) A named memory location in which a program can store intermediate results and from which it can read them.
(nautical) A shifting wind, or one that varies in force.
(nautical, in the plural) Those parts of the sea where a steady wind is not expected, especially the parts between the trade-wind belts.
